slides.0.title: Vineyard management, pests and diseases
slides.0.subtitle: Every vineyard choice trades off yield, quality and cost
slides.1.title: Training, pruning and the canopy
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Bush vines and trellising
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Bush vines (gobelet) need no wires, tolerate drought and shade the fruit, suiting hot dry areas, but are hard to mechanise; trellises such as VSP give even light and airflow and suit machinery
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Cane and spur pruning
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Cane pruning (e.g. Guyot) keeps one or two long canes each year and suits varieties with poorly fruitful basal buds; spur pruning (e.g. cordon) keeps many short spurs and is easier to manage and mechanise
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Canopy management
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Leaf removal exposes fruit and lowers pyrazines and disease, but too much causes sunburn; topping and shoot thinning control vigour. With warming, the new trend is to keep more leaves for shade
slides.1.content: Training and pruning fix bud numbers and light, and so yield and ripeness.
slides.2.title: Yield, rootstocks and phylloxera
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Yield and quality
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Too high a yield dilutes flavour and delays ripening, but “the lower the better” is not true either; the key is the balance of leaf area to fruit. Green harvesting before véraison adjusts the crop
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Phylloxera
slides.2.highlights.1.content: An aphid from North America that devastated European vineyards in the late 19th century by attacking vinifera roots. The solution, still standard worldwide, is grafting onto resistant American rootstocks
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Other uses of rootstocks
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Rootstocks also control vigour and adapt vines to limestone or saline soils, nematodes and drought. Sandy soils and isolated regions (e.g. Chile, Santorini) can often use own-rooted vines
slides.2.content: Own roots are no guarantee of quality and grafting is no quality problem; explain the risks and costs behind each.
slides.3.title: Diseases and farming philosophies
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Powdery and downy mildew
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Both came from North America to Europe in the 19th century. Powdery mildew (oidium) is controlled with sulphur and thrives in warm, shaded canopies; downy mildew needs rain and humidity and is controlled with copper (e.g. Bordeaux mixture)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Botrytis and viruses
slides.3.highlights.1.content: In humid conditions botrytis causes bunch rot; under the right conditions it becomes noble rot. Viruses such as leafroll (spread by mealybugs) and fanleaf (spread by nematodes) cannot be cured, only managed with clean stock and removal of infected vines
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Organic, biodynamic and sustainable
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Organic bans synthetic pesticides and fertilisers but allows copper and sulphur; biodynamics, from Rudolf Steiner’s 1924 lectures, adds preparations and a calendar; sustainability schemes assess environment, society and economics as a whole. Do not conflate the three
slides.3.content: Order for disease questions: climatic conditions → pathogen → effect on yield and quality → control and cost.
